\begin{abstract}
Trading agents built on large language models (LLMs) read news, so subtly edited news is an attack surface. Red-teaming studies report the attack success rate (ASR), the share of trading days on which an attacked agent decides differently from a clean run. We show that ASR conflates three effects: retrieval noise caused by adding \emph{any} documents to the agent's pool, behavioural-bias prompts that accompany the attack, and the content of the misinformation itself. We present \rhal{}, an offline, deterministic harness that trades an attacked agent and a clean twin in lockstep with common random numbers, records each attack for exact replay against every defence, and decomposes ASR with a ladder of placebo controls. Over \val{NseedsRun} paired simulated markets, the undefended agent's naive ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% splits into \val{MPlaceboNoneASR} percentage points (pp) of retrieval noise, \val{CmpDecBiasNone}\pp{} of bias prompts and \cmp{CmpDecMeaningNone} attributable to the misinformation's content, with a negligible remainder from the article count. Temporal grounding against market evidence and historical analogs lowers misinformation-driven (net) ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} at a cost of \val{CmpCostGrounded}\pp{} of clean-market return. Microstructure proxies add no detectable robustness on top of price-based grounding, and a hold-on-conflict risk rule slightly \emph{increases} misinformation-driven flips against an adaptive attacker. All claims rest on paired bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected permutation tests, and every no-lookahead guarantee, for prices and for text, is verified by tests that mutate the future.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
LLM agents, red teaming, financial misinformation, adversarial robustness, retrieval-augmented generation, negative controls, algorithmic trading
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
LLM-based trading agents such as FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem}, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} retrieve news from a memory store, reason over it together with market data, and emit sequential trading decisions~\cite{li2025investorbench,zhang2024finagent}. Their text inputs are an attack surface. Unlike a jailbreak, financial misinformation need not cross any safety boundary: a flipped direction word, an inflated percentage or a swapped cause produces text that still reads as plausible news, is hard to flag without a reference~\cite{jiang2026glisters}, and can change what the agent does. Poisoned retrieval corpora~\cite{zou2025poisonedrag} and injected third-party content~\cite{greshake2023indirect} are established threats to LLM applications; trading agents add a direct financial channel.

AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} formalised autonomous red-teaming of such agents. An attacker combines behavioural-bias prompts, minor semantic edits and style rewrites, filters candidates by similarity and detectability, and reinforces the strategies that changed the agent's decisions. Its headline metric, the ASR, reaches \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% for the undefended agent in our replication.

\textbf{The measurement problem.} ASR compares an attacked run with a clean run, but the two runs differ in more than the misinformation. The attacked agent's retrieval pool is larger, so different documents reach its top-$k$ even when the added text is harmless. It also receives the attacker's bias prompts. Comparisons between defences add two further confounds: arms that draw different attacker random numbers, and attacks that adapt differently to each defence. Epidemiology handles such confounding with \emph{negative controls}, i.e.\ exposures known to have no effect~\cite{lipsitch2010negative}; agent red-teaming has not used them.

\textbf{Approach.} We build a harness in which every confound is either held fixed or measured. An attacked agent and a clean twin trade the same market in lockstep. Attacker randomness is shared across arms, and each attack can be replayed bit-for-bit against every defence. A ladder of placebo controls adds the attack's ingredients one at a time, so consecutive differences isolate retrieval noise, article count, bias prompts and content. All conclusions are paired over \val{NseedsRun} simulated markets with bootstrap intervals and multiplicity-corrected tests.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}
\item A \emph{placebo-control ladder} that decomposes ASR into retrieval noise, article count, bias prompts and misinformation content; a \emph{frozen-attack replay} that confronts every defence with an identical recorded attack; and a \emph{one-step counterfactual ASR} that removes drift between the twins after the first disagreement (Sec.~\ref{sec:measure}).
\item \rhal{}, an offline, CPU-only, deterministic harness with common-random-number seeding, structural no-lookahead guarantees for prices \emph{and} text that are verified by future-mutation tests, and a paired statistical protocol (Sec.~\ref{sec:harness}).
\item Evidence that naive ASR overstates the effect of misinformation content \val{RatioNaiveToMeaning}-fold in this setting. Temporal grounding removes about \val{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} points of misinformation-driven ASR. Microstructure proxies and a risk layer add no detectable benefit on top, stronger grounding helps only marginally, and the risk layer's hold-on-conflict rule even backfires against an adaptive attacker (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{itemize}

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{LLM trading agents.} FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem} introduced layered memory and character design, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} coordinate multiple LLM roles, FinAgent~\cite{zhang2024finagent} adds multimodal tools, and InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench} standardises the perception--profile--memory--action design we follow. Finance-specific language models~\cite{araci2019finbert,wu2023bloomberggpt} and retrieval-augmented generation~\cite{lewis2020rag} supply the text channel these agents rely on.

\textbf{Attacks on LLM agents.} Knowledge-corruption attacks inject crafted passages into a retrieval corpus~\cite{zou2025poisonedrag}, and indirect prompt injection hides instructions in retrieved content~\cite{greshake2023indirect}. Automated red-teaming systems search over attack strategies~\cite{zhou2025autoredteamer,jiang2024artprompt}. For trading agents, TradeTrap~\cite{yan2025tradetrap} shows that small textual changes shift decisions, and AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, our base, adds a finance-structured operator space with closed-loop feedback.

\textbf{Financial misinformation.} Media tone moves markets~\cite{tetlock2007giving}, dictionary methods quantify it~\cite{loughran2011liability}, and counterfactual misinformation is hard to detect without a reference~\cite{jiang2026glisters,wang2026life}. Behavioural finance supplies the biases attackers exploit: overconfidence~\cite{barber2001boys}, loss aversion~\cite{kahneman1979prospect}, herding~\cite{spyrou2013herding} and noise trading~\cite{delong1990noise}.

\textbf{Experimental methodology.} Negative controls detect confounding in observational studies~\cite{lipsitch2010negative}. Common random numbers reduce the variance of simulation comparisons~\cite{law2015simulation}. Paired bootstrap intervals~\cite{efron1993bootstrap}, permutation tests~\cite{good2005permutation} and Holm's step-down correction~\cite{holm1979simple} support inference over seeds. Lookahead and backtest overfitting are the classic failure modes of trading research~\cite{lopezdeprado2018advances,bailey2014probability}.

\section{Threat Model and Harness}\label{sec:harness}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_harness.tex}
\caption{The paired red-teaming harness. An attacked agent (top) and an identical clean twin (bottom) trade the same market in lockstep and differ only in the text they read. MisGen injects edited copies of the day's news and sets a bias prompt in the attacked agent's context. Both agents may use the same defences, which are ablated one at a time. A day on which the two decisions differ is a \emph{flip}; the share of flipped days is the ASR. In the adaptive setting, strategies retrieved on flipped days are reinforced.}
\label{fig:harness}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{Setting and attacker.} Each day $t$ the market publishes a set $\mathcal{N}_t$ of news items about one asset. An agent retrieves the top-$k$ relevant items from the last few days, combines them with market observations, and chooses $a_t\in\{\text{Buy},\text{Sell},\text{Hold}\}$, executed at the next day's open. The attacker can add documents to the agent's news pool and place a behavioural-bias prompt in its context, but cannot touch prices, the agent's code or the clean news. Its goal is to change decisions. Following AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, MisGen builds each candidate from three operator spaces: a \emph{bias} prompt (overconfidence, loss aversion, anchoring, herding or confirmation); a \emph{minor edit} of one of eight types (direction flip, sentiment shift, numerical, temporal, entity, concept, causal or vague attribution); and an optional \emph{style rewrite} (news or academic register). A candidate is kept only if its TF-IDF similarity to the source is at least $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}$ and a detectability classifier scores it below a threshold calibrated to a \val{DetFPR}\% false-positive rate on clean text. Strategies are sampled from a P\'olya urn,
\begin{equation}
P(s)\propto 1+\alpha\, h_s,
\end{equation}
where $h_s$ counts how often strategy $s$ was retrieved on a day whose decision flipped~\cite{mahmoud2008polya}.

\textbf{Paired simulation.} Every run drives two agents over the same market path (Fig.~\ref{fig:harness}). The \emph{treated} agent reads clean and injected news under the attacker's bias prompt; the \emph{shadow} agent is an identical clean twin. Both have their own portfolio, memory and risk layer, so a flip is a paired, same-day comparison.

\textbf{Agent.} Following InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench}, the agent has perception, profile, memory and action modules. Our experiments use a transparent surrogate policy that scores each retrieved document with a negation- and intensity-aware finance lexicon~\cite{loughran2011liability}. It forms a retrieval-weighted text signal $s_{\mathrm{text}}$, applies the day's bias as an explicit parameter shift (e.g.\ overconfidence lowers the action threshold, loss aversion amplifies negative signals by $1.7$), and fuses
\begin{equation}
s=\lambda\,s_{\mathrm{text}}+(1-\lambda)\,s_{\mathrm{mkt}},\qquad \lambda=0.75,
\end{equation}
to mimic an LLM's text-heavy reaction. It buys or sells when $|s|$ exceeds a threshold of $0.15$. A real-LLM policy with identical prompts and cached responses runs in the same harness.

\textbf{Defences.} \emph{Temporal grounding} compares text with market evidence $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}=\tanh(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_t)$, built from trailing-normalised trend, volatility, drawdown and momentum features and blended with the mean forward return of the $k$ most similar past windows. It shrinks inconsistent text toward the evidence:
\begin{equation}
s_g=s-\kappa\,(1-c)\,(s-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}),\qquad c=1-\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert s_{\mathrm{text}}-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}\rvert.
\end{equation}
An analog window ending at $e$ is admissible on day $t$ only if $e+H\le t$, so its $H$-day outcome is already known. \emph{Microstructure proxies} add a range-based spread~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, order-flow imbalance~\cite{cont2014price}, volume shock and Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity} to the evidence. A \emph{risk layer} applies after the policy and can only shrink or close positions: a confidence gate, \emph{hold-on-conflict} (no new trade when $c<0.6$), volatility-targeted sizing, stop-loss and take-profit, and a drawdown throttle.

\textbf{No lookahead, determinism.} Features are $z$-scored over trailing windows, orders fill at the next open, analogs obey $e+H\le t$, and the retrieval TF-IDF and the attacker's similarity filter are fit only on news dated before the evaluation window. Tests multiply all prices after a cut-off by five, or replace every article dated after it, and require bit-identical decisions before the cut-off. All randomness flows from seeds derived by hashing (master seed, component, day, item). The attacker is seeded by its injection type rather than by the arm, so every arm of a seed draws the same attacker random numbers: common random numbers~\cite{law2015simulation}.

% =============================================================================
\section{Measuring Attack Success}\label{sec:measure}
\textbf{Metrics.} The misinformation exposure rate (MER) is the share of retrieved documents that are synthetic. The attack success rate is the share of evaluation days $\mathcal{T}$ with a flip,
\begin{equation}
\asr=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[a_t\neq a_t^{\mathrm{clean}}\right].
\end{equation}
\emph{Active} ASR counts only flips in which the treated agent trades. It discounts the defensive Holds a risk layer creates, which plain ASR scores as attack successes.

\textbf{Control ladder.} To separate what the misinformation \emph{says} from the side effects of injecting it, we add the attack's ingredients one at a time on top of identical retrieval, seeds and tapes (Fig.~\ref{fig:controls}):
\begin{equation}
\asr_{\mathrm{attack}}=\underbrace{\asr_{\mathrm{plc}}}_{\text{retrieval noise}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{count}}}_{\text{article count}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{bias}}}_{\text{bias prompts}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}}_{\text{content}}.
\end{equation}
The \emph{placebo} injects a meaning-preserving paraphrase of every clean item: synonym and connector substitutions that never touch directions, numbers, entities or causes. The \emph{count-matched} placebo paraphrases only the items the attack actually injected. The \emph{bias-matched} placebo adds the attack's daily bias prompts. The attack adds the content. All placebo variants draw the same paraphrase for a given (day, item), so each control's pool is a subset of the previous one's. The conventional \emph{net ASR}, $\asr_{\mathrm{attack}}-\asr_{\mathrm{plc}}$, still contains $\Delta_{\mathrm{count}}+\Delta_{\mathrm{bias}}$. $\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}$ is the effect of the misinformation itself.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_controls.tex}
\caption{The control ladder. Each arm adds one ingredient of the attack to the previous one, with the same seed, market and recorded attack, so consecutive differences isolate one component of ASR.}
\label{fig:controls}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Adaptive and frozen attacks.} In the \emph{adaptive} setting the attacker's feedback loop runs against the defended agent. In the \emph{frozen} setting the attack recorded against the undefended agent, i.e.\ its documents and daily bias prompts, is replayed verbatim against every defence. Differences between frozen arms are therefore caused by the defence alone. Replaying the tape against its own source agent must reproduce that run exactly, and the pipeline checks this on every seed.

\textbf{One-step counterfactual ASR.} After the first flip the twins' portfolios and memories differ, so later flips may reflect accumulated state rather than the day's text. Each day, a throw-away copy of the agent therefore decides with deep copies of the clean twin's memory and portfolio but with the treated agent's documents and bias. cf-ASR is its disagreement rate with the twin. It only reads copies, so it leaves every other quantity bit-identical, which is tested.

\textbf{Statistics.} The unit of replication is a seed, i.e.\ one simulated market with its own news, prices and attacker draws. All arms of a seed share the market path, so every comparison is paired by seed. We report the mean per-seed difference with a 95\% percentile-bootstrap interval ($10^4$ resamples)~\cite{efron1993bootstrap} and a two-sided sign-flip permutation $p$-value (exact for $n\le 16$, otherwise $2\times10^4$ random flips)~\cite{good2005permutation}, Holm-corrected within each family of related comparisons~\cite{holm1979simple}. We call a difference \emph{detectable} only if its interval excludes zero \emph{and} $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.05$.

% =============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
\textbf{Data.} Each seed generates \val{NDays} business days of synthetic OHLCV from a three-regime Markov drift with GARCH(1,1) volatility~\cite{bollerslev1986garch}, and \val{NewsPerDay} template news items per day about a fictitious company. The items' latent sentiment correlates ($\rho=0.35$) with the next day's return, so news is genuinely but noisily informative. Every template contains an entity, a figure, a cause and a period, so each edit type has a target. The last \val{NevalDays} days are evaluated, matching AutoRedTrader's 60-day window, and the rest serve as warm-up and analog library.

\textbf{Configuration.} Retrieval is TF-IDF top-\val{TopK} over the last three days with recency decay. Grounding uses 30-day windows, $5$ analogs, horizon $H=5$ and $\kappa=\val{Kappa}$. MisGen uses bias probability $0.7$, $\alpha=1$, $K=3$ attempts, $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.35$ and one candidate per clean item. Trades pay \val{FeeBps}\,bp fees and \val{SlipBps}\,bp slippage, long-only and without leverage.

\textbf{Arms.} Per seed and defence level (none; grounding with microstructure proxies; grounding plus risk layer) we run a clean arm, the adaptive attack, its frozen replay, and the three placebo controls: 18 paired arms per seed over \val{NseedsRun} seeds. Ablations remove one attack component (minor edits, detector filtering, bias prompts, feedback, rewriting) or vary the defence (price-only grounding, microstructure proxies, risk layer alone or on top, hold-on-conflict), the retrieval breadth $k\in\{2,4,8\}$ and the grounding strength $\kappa\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}$, each with its own placebo and, for defences, a frozen replay. The full study runs on one laptop CPU core in about 1.5 hours.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
\IfFileExists{tables/tab_main.tex}{\input{tables/tab_main.tex}}{}

\subsection{How much of the attack is the misinformation?}
Against the undefended agent the attack reaches an MER of \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% (\val{MInjectedNoneMERLift}$\times$ the synthetic share of the visible pool) and a naive ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% (Table~\ref{tab:main}). This is higher than the 26.7\% reported on Bitcoin~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, but the settings differ (synthetic data, a surrogate agent, rule-based operators), and neither figure is corrected for placebo effects.

The placebo alone, paraphrases that change no fact, flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions. Adding documents reshuffles the agent's top-$k$, near-duplicates displace other items, and decisions near the action threshold flip. The control ladder (Fig.~\ref{fig:decomposition}) attributes the rest. Matching the article count adds nothing detectable (\cmp{CmpDecCountNone}, \pholm{CmpDecCountNone}). The attacker's bias prompts add \cmp{CmpDecBiasNone} (\pholm{CmpDecBiasNone}). The content of the misinformation adds \cmp{CmpDecMeaningNone} (\pholm{CmpDecMeaningNone}), about \val{ShareMeaningOfNaive}\% of the naive ASR. The conventional net ASR of \val{CmpNetNone}\% \ci{CmpNetNone} is thus inflated by the bias prompts, and naive ASR overstates the effect of the content \val{RatioNaiveToMeaning}-fold.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_decomposition.pdf}
\caption{ASR decomposed by the control ladder on the frozen attack (mean over \val{NseedsRun} seeds). Bars sum to the attack's ASR; the article-count component is at most \val{DecCountMaxAbs}\,pp in size and too small to see. Grounding shrinks both the retrieval noise and the content effect.}
\label{fig:decomposition}
\end{figure}

Two checks show that this conclusion does not depend on how flips are counted. The one-step counterfactual ASR, which re-scores every day from the clean twin's own state, stays close to the sequential ASR: the gap is \cmp{CmpCfGapNone} for the undefended agent (\pholm{CmpCfGapNone}) and \cmp{CmpCfGapGroundedRisk} with the risk layer (\pholm{CmpCfGapGroundedRisk}). Drift between the twins therefore inflates ASR by less than one point. The fully matched counterfactual estimate of the content effect, \cmp{CmpCfMeaningNone}, agrees with $\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}$. Fig.~\ref{fig:replay} shows one market: the attacked, undefended agent and its twin disagree on \val{ReplayFlipsNone} of \val{ReplayDays} days, and on \val{ReplayFlipsGrounded} with grounding under the identical recorded attack.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_forest.pdf}
\caption{Paired effects over \val{NseedsRun} seeds (points: mean per-seed difference; bars: 95\% bootstrap CIs; filled: detectable after Holm correction). (a) Reduction in net ASR from each defence component, positive is more robust. (b, c) Change in net ASR and in MER when each attack component is present.}
\label{fig:forest}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Defences}
Temporal grounding is the only defence with a large effect (Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}a). It lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} against the adaptive attacker (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet}) and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against the frozen one (\pholm{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet}), so its benefit does not depend on the attacker adapting. Part of the gain is lower sensitivity to \emph{any} pool perturbation: grounding also lowers placebo ASR, by \cmp{CmpPlaceboGrounded}. But it also cuts the content effect from \val{CmpDecMeaningNone} to \cmp{CmpDecMeaningGrounded}, and cuts placebo-corrected active flips by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet} (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet}). It does not neutralise the attack: the grounded agent's net ASR is still \val{CmpNetGrounded}\% \ci{CmpNetGrounded}. The price is \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} of clean-market return (Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier}): the synthetic news is genuinely informative, and grounding discounts true stories that the lagging market evidence does not yet support.

Price-only grounding delivers almost all of this gain: adding the microstructure proxies changes net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveMicro} (adaptive) and \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenMicro} (frozen), neither detectable. In our generator, high, low and volume are functions of the simulated return and volatility plus independent noise, so the proxies carry no directional information beyond the price path.

The risk layer behaves differently on its own and on top of grounding. Alone it lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone} (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone}). On top of grounding it \emph{raises} net ASR against the adaptive attacker by \cmpneg{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet} (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet}) and placebo-corrected active flips by \cmpneg{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskActnet}, with no detectable drawdown benefit (\cmp{CmpDdRisk}, \pholm{CmpDdRisk}). The hold-on-conflict rule accounts for the increase: removing it lowers net ASR by \cmpneg{CmpAblDefAdaptiveHold} (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveHold}). Holding whenever text and market conflict changes the attacked agent's decision on exactly the days the injected text creates a conflict, which its clean twin, trading on genuine news, does not do. Against the frozen attack, the change in net ASR from adding the risk layer is not detectable (\cmp{CmpGainFrozenRiskNet}).


\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_frontier.pdf}
\caption{Robustness--return frontier: net ASR under the adaptive attack against the clean-market return of the same defence (mean and 95\% CIs over \val{NseedsRun} seeds). Grounding moves the agent left at a cost in return; microstructure proxies and the risk layer do not move it further.}
\label{fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

\subsection{What drives the attack}
Three components detectably strengthen the attack's decision impact (Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}b): the minor edits themselves (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoMinorNet}), detector filtering (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFilteringNet}) and the bias prompts (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoBiasNet}), the last consistent with $\Delta_{\mathrm{bias}}$ above. Filtering helps because, without it, the first candidate is always accepted, including the causal and vague-attribution edits that the detector almost always flags (Table~\ref{tab:detector}). Strategy feedback and style rewriting raise exposure instead (Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}c): MER rises by \val{CmpAblAttackWoFeedbackMer}\pp{} and \val{CmpAblAttackWoRewriteMer}\pp{}, but neither changes net ASR detectably. The P\'olya urn rewards strategies that were \emph{retrieved} on flipped days, and with a placebo floor near \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% its flip signal is mostly noise. It therefore learns what gets retrieved, not what changes decisions.

\textbf{Robustness to retrieval breadth and grounding strength.} Net ASR is higher only with the narrowest retrieval ($k=2$ vs.\ $4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKTwoNet}; $8$ vs.\ $4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKEightNet}). The placebo floor falls with $k$ (\cmp{CmpAblRetKEightPlacebo} from $k=4$ to $8$) as the text signal averages over more documents. Grounding strength matters little: only the step from $\kappa=0.7$ to $1.0$ against the adaptive attacker lowers net ASR detectably (\cmp{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropSevenOnepZero}, \pholm{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropSevenOnepZero}), and each step costs about \val{CmpAblKappaCostZeropSevenOnepZero}\pp{} of clean return.

\centering

\caption{One simulated market (seed \val{ReplaySeed}) under the same recorded attack. Filled triangles are the agent's trades, outlines its clean twin's, and shaded days are flips. Grounding (b) keeps the agent closer to its twin than no defence (a).}

% =============================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
\textbf{Report placebo-corrected ASR.} In our setting, \val{ShareNoiseOfNaive}\% of the flips that naive ASR attributes to the attack also occur with harmless paraphrases. Misinformation studies should report a placebo and, where an attack bundles several ingredients, a matched ladder. Defence comparisons should share attacker random numbers or replay a recorded attack. Otherwise arm-to-arm attack noise is as large as the defence effects: before we keyed attacker seeds by injection type, identically configured arms differed by up to 8.6 points of ASR.

\textbf{Limitations.} (i)~The agent is a transparent surrogate, not an LLM. The harness runs real LLM policies unchanged, but absolute rates, and possibly the ranking of defences, may differ. (ii)~Prices and news are synthetic, and template news is more regular than real reporting, which likely makes the lexical detector easier both to train and to evade. The microstructure null result in particular needs real order-flow data. (iii)~The detectability filter is a small feature classifier (training accuracy \val{DetAcc}) standing in for an LLM judge. (iv)~Stops are evaluated at daily closes. (v)~Each seed evaluates only 60 days, so we rely on paired differences over \val{NseedsRun} seeds, not single runs.

% =============================================================================
\section{Ethics and Safety}\label{sec:ethics}
This work generates synthetic financial misinformation only to measure and improve robustness. The market and the company are fictitious. Every generated document carries a mandatory provenance label and a safety tag, and generated text never leaves the simulator: our figures and replay viewer show only labels such as edit type, never generated text. The harness has no broker connection or order-routing path, the attacker's objective is decision change rather than profit, and no component disseminates content. We release the framework for defensive research and discourage its use on real news feeds.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
Attack success rates for misinformation against LLM trading agents bundle retrieval noise, bias prompts and content. With matched placebo controls, shared attacker randomness and paired statistics over \val{NseedsRun} markets, the content of the misinformation accounts for \cmp{CmpDecMeaningNone} of a \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% naive ASR. Temporal grounding is the only defence that substantially reduces it. Stronger grounding helps only marginally, and microstructure proxies and a hold-on-conflict risk layer do not help further. We hope the control ladder becomes standard practice for reporting attacks on retrieval-based agents. Next steps are real-LLM policies, real price and order-flow data, and adaptive attackers that target the grounding signal directly.
